title: Portuguese foundations
description: Four A1 Brazilian Portuguese lessons: first words, introductions, polite café requests, and numbers for everyday quantities. Native-speaker editorial review remains open.

units.title: Getting around
units.objective: Understand prices and quantities in everyday errands.

units.title: Finding your way
units.objective: Ask where things are and follow spoken directions.

units.title: Everyday life
units.objective: Talk about days, times, and the people around you.

concepts.title: First words and greetings
concepts.explanation: Portuguese grew from Latin on the Atlantic edge of Iberia, and thousands of everyday words came into both Portuguese and English from Latin — nação, informação, restaurante, café. You can already recognize them before you speak a word of Portuguese. The words below are the first ones to say out loud: olá opens almost every conversation, obrigado answers kindness, sim and não steer it. Men say obrigado, women say obrigada — match the ending to yourself.
concepts.commonError: Say olá the moment you arrive. Men say obrigado and women say obrigada; day-zero learners are understood either way.

concepts.title: Introducing yourself
concepts.explanation: This course practices Brazilian Portuguese. Meu nome é introduces your name: Meu nome é Ana. Sou means I am and also works for an introduction: Sou Ana. Learn Qual é o seu nome? as a complete question for asking a name. Prazer is a short, friendly response when you meet someone.
concepts.commonError: Keep é in Meu nome é Ana. The accent belongs to the word é (is); e without an accent means and.

concepts.title: Polite café requests
concepts.explanation: Eu gostaria de means I would like. Keep de before the item: Eu gostaria de um café, por favor. Both café and chá take um in these requests. You can omit eu because gostaria supplies enough context: Gostaria de um café, por favor. A short Um café, por favor also works. Obrigado or obrigada expresses thanks; use the form that fits how you refer to yourself.

examples.target: Eu gostaria de um café, por favor.
examples.meaning: I would like a coffee, please.

examples.target: Eu gostaria de um chá, por favor.
examples.meaning: I would like a tea, please.

concepts.commonError: Keep de after gostaria: gostaria de um café. Chá means tea and keeps its accent.

concepts.title: Numbers and quantities
concepts.explanation: Learn Brazilian Portuguese numbers as two short runs, then use quanto custa to ask the price of one thing. Use dois with masculine cafés and duas with feminine maçãs. The item tells you which form you need.

examples.meaning: How much does a coffee cost?

concepts.commonError: Use duas with maçãs and dois with cafés. Keep quanto custa as one learned price question.

concepts.title: Asking the way
concepts.explanation: Onde means where. Portuguese often asks about a place with ficar, which means to stay or to be situated: Onde fica a estação? Directions come as short chunks worth learning whole: em frente (straight ahead), à esquerda (to the left), à direita (to the right). The accent on à is a contraction of a plus a, and it is what makes the phrase mean to the left rather than the left. Starting with Desculpe turns a bare question into a polite one.

examples.meaning: Straight ahead, then to the left.
Excuse me, where is the bathroom?

concepts.commonError: Onde asks where. Quem asks who and o que asks what. Keep the accent on à, which distinguishes to the left from the left.

concepts.title: Prices and paying
concepts.explanation: Quanto custa asks how much something costs, and it is the standard price question. Answer with a number and euros. Caro means expensive and barato means inexpensive. To disagree, put não before the verb: Não é caro. The bill is a conta, a feminine noun, and por favor turns it into a request.

examples.meaning: How much does the coffee cost?

concepts.commonError: Não goes before the verb. Portuguese also uses isto for this as a standalone thing, and este before a noun.

concepts.title: Days and times
concepts.explanation: Hoje means today and amanhã means tomorrow. Portuguese weekdays are numbered rather than named: segunda-feira is the second fair, Monday, and the sequence runs to sexta-feira. They are feminine and take na when you mean on that day: na segunda-feira, on Monday. Amanhã also carries the meaning of morning in some phrases, and the article separates them.
concepts.commonError: Use na with feminine weekdays: na segunda-feira. The tildes on amanhã and the hyphen in segunda-feira both matter.

concepts.title: Family and people
concepts.explanation: Portuguese nouns are masculine or feminine, and the article changes with them: o irmão (brother), a irmã (sister), os pais (parents). The verb ter is irregular in the I form: tenho, I have. Possessives normally take an article, which English does not do: a minha família is my family, literally the my family, and os meus pais is my parents.

examples.target: Os meus pais vivem em Lisboa.

concepts.commonError: Portuguese keeps the article with a possessive: a minha família, not minha família. It is one of the commonest things learners drop.

vocabulary.example: Eu gostaria de um café, por favor.
Os meus pais vivem em Lisboa.

lessons.title: First words
lessons.objective: Recognize and say your first Portuguese words — greetings and Latin-shared words — before building any sentences.
lessons.explanation: You already know hundreds of Portuguese words: nação, informação, restaurante. They came into English and Portuguese from Latin, the common root of Portuguese, Spanish, French and Italian — which is why the Romance languages resemble each other. Today you only say a few out loud: olá, obrigado, sim, não. No sentences yet — those come next.
lessons.culturalNote: Olá works everywhere, all day. Obrigado ends in -o when men say it and -a (obrigada) when women say it.

exercises.prompt: You already know this word — friends say it a dozen times a day in Lisbon. «Olá» — what does it mean?
exercises.explanation: Olá. is hello — the first word to say out loud. The rest of this lesson stays this small.

exercises.prompt: Think: you meet a friend in Lisbon. One word greets them before anything else. Say it in your head — then write it.
exercises.explanation: Olá. One word, said first, opens the conversation.

exercises.prompt: Nação, informação, restaurante — spelled almost the same in English and Portuguese. Why do you already recognize them?
answers: Portuguese and English share thousands of words from Latin.
options: Portuguese and English share thousands of words from Latin.
Portuguese borrowed its everyday words from modern English.
exercises.explanation: Both languages inherited these words from Latin — the common root of the Romance languages. Recognition comes before production.

exercises.prompt: Give the English meaning: Obrigado.
exercises.explanation: Obrigado is thank you — the second word to say out loud.

exercises.prompt: Complete the first word you say to a friend: ___
exercises.explanation: Olá. — said before everything else.

exercises.prompt: Read the exchange. How many times do you read the word for thank you?
exercises.passage: — Olá ! — Olá. — Obrigado ? — Sim, obrigado. — Não, obrigado.
exercises.explanation: Every word on this page is one you already learned.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the model: first words.
exercises.explanation: Two words you can say. Replay slowly, then at normal speed.

lessons.title: Introducing yourself

exercises.prompt: Which phrase asks another person their name in Brazilian Portuguese?
exercises.explanation: Use the complete name question when meeting someone.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to introduce Ana by name.
exercises.explanation: Keep é in Meu nome é Ana. The accent belongs to the word é (is); e without an accent means and.

exercises.prompt: Read the first meeting. Who gives their own name?
exercises.explanation: The person who uses the name phrase introduces themself.
exercises.passage:
Ana: Olá. Meu nome é Ana.
Leo: Olá. Prazer.
exercises.translation:
Ana: Hello. My name is Ana.
Leo: Hello. Nice to meet you.

exercises.prompt: Say “Nice to meet you” using the short expression taught here.
exercises.explanation: Use this short response after an introduction.

exercises.prompt: Imagine meeting a new classmate. Introduce yourself as Ana, using the phrase that means “My name is”.
exercises.explanation: Keep é in Meu nome é Ana. The accent belongs to the word é (is); e without an accent means and.

exercises.prompt: Ask a peer “What is your name?” using the complete question taught here.
exercises.explanation: This is the name question from the lesson; recall it as a whole.

lessons.objective: Choose a drink and make a polite café request from memory.

You can omit eu because gostaria supplies enough context: Gostaria de um café, por favor. A short Um café, por favor also works. Obrigado or obrigada expresses thanks; use the form that fits how you refer to yourself.

examples.target: Eu gostaria de um café, por favor.
examples.meaning: I would like a coffee, please.

examples.target: Eu gostaria de um chá, por favor.
examples.meaning: I would like a tea, please.

lessons.culturalNote: These café requests use Brazilian Portuguese. The lessons accept both explicit eu and its omission in the full request.

exercises.prompt: You want tea. Which complete request matches your intention?
answers: Eu gostaria de um chá, por favor.
exercises.explanation: Change the drink while keeping the polite request frame.
options: Eu gostaria de um café, por favor.
Eu gostaria de um chá, por favor.

exercises.prompt: Build the full polite request for one coffee.
answers: Eu gostaria de um café, por favor.
exercises.explanation: Keep de after gostaria: gostaria de um café. Chá means tea and keeps its accent.

exercises.prompt: Read the café exchange. Which drink does the customer request?
exercises.explanation: The customer requests tea; the thanks closes the exchange.
exercises.passage:
Customer: Olá. Um chá, por favor.
Server: Um chá?
Customer: Sim. Obrigada.
exercises.translation:
Customer: Hello. A tea, please.
Server: A tea?
Customer: Yes. Thank you.

exercises.prompt: Say “I would like a tea, please” using the full request frame.
answers: Eu gostaria de um chá, por favor.
Gostaria de um chá, por favor.
exercises.explanation: Keep de after gostaria: gostaria de um café. Chá means tea and keeps its accent.

exercises.prompt: You arrive at a café and want coffee. Make the short request “A coffee, please”.
exercises.explanation: The short request still includes please.

exercises.prompt: Give the English meaning of this complete request: Eu gostaria de um café, por favor.
answers: I would like a coffee, please.
exercises.explanation: This is a polite request, not a statement about having coffee.

lessons.title: Numbers and quantities
lessons.objective: Recognize one to ten, ask a price, and order a small quantity.
lessons.explanation: Count one through ten as two short runs. Then use quanto custa for a price and choose dois or duas from the noun that follows.

examples.meaning: How much does a coffee cost?

lessons.culturalNote: In Brazil, prices and quantities arrive quickly in ordinary errands. Hear the number first, then the item.

exercises.prompt: Which Brazilian Portuguese number means three?
exercises.explanation: Três is three.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to ask the price of one coffee.
exercises.explanation: Quanto custa asks what one thing costs.

exercises.prompt: Say in Brazilian Portuguese: Two apples, please.
exercises.explanation: Maçãs is feminine, so use duas.

exercises.prompt: Think: you want one coffee. Ask its price, then write the question.
exercises.explanation: The learned price question is Quanto custa, followed by the item.

lessons.title: Asking the way
lessons.objective: Ask where something is and follow a two-step direction.
lessons.explanation: Onde means where. Portuguese often asks about a place with ficar, which means to stay or to be situated: Onde fica a estação? Directions come as short chunks worth learning whole: em frente (straight ahead), à esquerda (to the left), à direita (to the right). The accent on à is a contraction of a plus a, and it is what makes the phrase mean to the left rather than the left. Starting with Desculpe turns a bare question into a polite one.

examples.meaning: Straight ahead, then to the left.
Excuse me, where is the bathroom?

lessons.culturalNote: Ouça and Desculpe both open a request in Portugal; in Brazil you will hear Com licença just as often.

exercises.prompt: You need to ask where something is. Which word does that?
exercises.explanation: Onde asks about a place. Quem asks who, and o que asks what.

exercises.prompt: Read the exchange. Which direction comes first?
exercises.explanation: The first instruction is em frente; à esquerda comes after depois, as the second step.
exercises.passage:
Turista: Desculpe, onde fica a estação?
Transeunte: Em frente, depois à esquerda.
Turista: Obrigado!
exercises.translation:
Tourist: Excuse me, where is the station?
Passer-by: Straight ahead, then to the left.
Tourist: Thank you!

exercises.prompt: Build the question that asks where the station is.
exercises.explanation: Ficar is the usual verb for where something is situated, and estação is feminine, so the article is a.

exercises.prompt: Ask where the bathroom is.
exercises.explanation: Banheiro is masculine, so the article is o.

exercises.prompt: Complete the directions: Em frente, depois à ___
exercises.explanation: Esquerda is left. Direita would send the learner the other way.

exercises.prompt: Make the question polite by putting Desculpe in front: Onde fica a estação?
exercises.explanation: Desculpe leads the sentence and a comma separates it from the question.

lessons.title: Prices and paying
lessons.objective: Ask what something costs, react to the price, and ask for the bill.

To disagree, put não before the verb: Não é caro. The bill is a conta, a feminine noun, and por favor turns it into a request.

examples.meaning: How much does the coffee cost?

lessons.culturalNote: In Portuguese cafés the bill usually arrives when you ask for it, so a conta, por favor ends the visit.

exercises.prompt: Which question asks the price of something?
exercises.explanation: Quanto asks how much and custa comes from custar, to cost.

exercises.prompt: Say that it is not expensive: É caro.
exercises.explanation: Não goes before the verb in Portuguese.

exercises.prompt: You want to know what a coffee costs. Ask the question.
exercises.explanation: Custa is singular because one coffee is being priced.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that says this is very expensive.
exercises.explanation: Muito means very and it sits directly before the adjective.

exercises.prompt: Ask for the bill.
exercises.explanation: Conta is feminine, so the article is a.

exercises.prompt: Complete the price question: ___ custa o café?
exercises.explanation: Quanto custa is the fixed frame for asking a price.

lessons.title: Days and times
lessons.objective: Name days, place an action on a day, and say what today is.
lessons.explanation: Hoje means today and amanhã means tomorrow. Portuguese weekdays are numbered rather than named: segunda-feira is the second fair, Monday, and the sequence runs to sexta-feira. They are feminine and take na when you mean on that day: na segunda-feira, on Monday. Amanhã also carries the meaning of morning in some phrases, and the article separates them.
lessons.culturalNote: The numbered weekdays come from the church calendar, where Sunday was the first fair and Monday the second.

exercises.prompt: Which word means today?
exercises.explanation: Hoje is today. Amanhã is tomorrow, and segunda is Monday.

exercises.prompt: Read the week. What day is it today?
exercises.explanation: Hoje é quarta-feira gives the answer directly in the third sentence.
exercises.passage: Na segunda-feira trabalho. Na terça-feira aprendo português. Hoje é quarta-feira. Amanhã é quinta-feira.
exercises.translation: On Monday I work. On Tuesday I learn Portuguese. Today is Wednesday. Tomorrow is Thursday.

exercises.prompt: According to the week you just read, which day comes next?
exercises.explanation: Amanhã é quinta-feira names the following day.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that says today is Wednesday.
exercises.explanation: Hoje first, then é, then the day, with its hyphen intact.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: Amanhã ___ quinta-feira.
exercises.explanation: The same frame as Hoje é quarta-feira, with amanhã in place of hoje.

exercises.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: today is Monday.
exercises.explanation: Hoje é plus the day name, the same frame as the model.

exercises.prompt: Give the English meaning: Na segunda-feira trabalho.
exercises.explanation: Portuguese marks on with na before a feminine weekday rather than a separate word.

lessons.title: Family and people
lessons.objective: Name close family members and say who you have, with the right article.
lessons.explanation: Portuguese nouns are masculine or feminine, and the article changes with them: o irmão (brother), a irmã (sister), os pais (parents). The verb ter is irregular in the I form: tenho, I have. Possessives normally take an article, which English does not do: a minha família is my family, literally the my family, and os meus pais is my parents.

examples.target: Os meus pais vivem em Lisboa.

lessons.culturalNote: A família in Portuguese often includes grandparents and cousins, and it is the standard answer to tell me about yourself.

exercises.prompt: Which one means the sister?
exercises.explanation: Irmã is the sister. Irmão is the brother, and pais are the parents.

exercises.prompt: Predict the form before you write it: I have a brother.
exercises.explanation: Ter is irregular, so the I form is tenho rather than tene.

exercises.prompt: Which one is correct for I have a sister?
exercises.explanation: Irmã is feminine, so the article is uma.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that says this is my family.
exercises.explanation: Portuguese keeps the article with the possessive, so it is a minha família.

exercises.prompt: Change one sister into two sisters: Tenho uma irmã.
exercises.explanation: The plural adds -s to irmã, and uma becomes duas.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: Os meus ___ vivem em Lisboa.
exercises.explanation: Pais is plural, and it still takes the article os with the possessive.

exercises.prompt: Read about the family. Where do the parents live?
exercises.explanation: The last sentence places the parents in Lisbon.
exercises.passage: A minha família é pequena. O meu irmão chama-se Max. A minha irmã chama-se Ana. Os meus pais vivem em Lisboa.
exercises.translation: My family is small. My brother is called Max. My sister is called Ana. My parents live in Lisbon.
